# Inference-Compute Budget vs. Attack Step Completion: Replication Across Model Families

**Problem:** The AISI 2026 finding that performance scales log-linearly with inference-time compute (10M→100M tokens yields up to 59% gains) has only been documented on a narrow set of frontier models. It is unknown whether this scaling law holds for open-weight models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen families).

**Direction:** Replicate the AISI inference-token budget experiment using open-weight models on a simplified 5-10 step cyber range (e.g., a local CTF-style Metasploitable VM chain). Vary token budget from 1K to 500K across model families and plot steps completed vs. log(tokens). Test whether log-linear scaling is a universal phenomenon or specific to frontier closed models.

**Why it matters:** If log-linear scaling is universal, even cheap open-weight models become significantly more dangerous with increased inference budget. If it is not, this tells evaluators which model families pose greater scaling risk. Directly addresses the lack of longitudinal cross-model comparison methodology.

**Relevant context:** Folkerts et al. 2026 (AISI) found log-linear scaling with no plateau: steps completed rose from 1.7 (GPT-4o) to 9.8 (Opus 4.6) over 18 months at fixed 10M token budget. At 100M tokens, Opus 4.6 averaged 1.4/7 ICS steps. The study covered only 7 frontier models. Open-weight replication would extend findings. (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214)

# Copilot vs. Autonomous: Measuring the Amplification Factor in Guided Cyber Attack Scenarios

**Problem:** MITRE OCCULT identifies the human-AI copilot paradigm as the most realistic near-term threat but the least studied. Almost all existing evaluations measure fully autonomous AI performance. We have no data quantifying how much a human operator amplifies AI performance on multi-step tasks.

**Direction:** Design a controlled study where CS students with no security background (1) attempt a 5-step CTF-style challenge alone, (2) use an LLM autonomously, and (3) use an LLM in copilot mode (human provides high-level decisions, AI executes). Measure steps completed, time, and errors in each condition. Compute a 'copilot amplification factor'.

**Why it matters:** The copilot threat model is most relevant for real attackers yet least benchmarked. Measuring amplification quantitatively would directly fill the gap identified by OCCULT and inform policy thresholds: is a novice + AI equivalent to an expert alone?

**Relevant context:** MITRE OCCULT (arxiv.org/abs/2502.15797) argues CTF-only evaluations miss copilot scenarios. HTB AI Range (Dec 2025) benchmarks AI agents and human-AI teaming side-by-side. Hack The Box reports AI matched hundreds of human teams on 19/20 easy challenges but humans outperformed on multi-step finals.

# Bottleneck Taxonomy Replication: Do DeepMind's Blind Spots Hold Across Newer Models?

**Problem:** Rodriguez et al. 2025 (DeepMind) identified evasion, persistence, and obfuscation as systematic blind spots in current AI cyber evaluations, grounded in analysis of 12K real incidents. It is unknown whether these blind spots persist in the model generations released after that study (e.g., Claude Opus 4.6, GPT-5 class models).

**Direction:** Create a mini-benchmark of 20 challenges: 10 covering the identified blind-spot categories (evasion, persistence, obfuscation) and 10 from well-covered categories (initial access, exploitation). Run 3-4 current frontier API models and compute success rates per category. Compare ratios to Rodriguez et al.'s baseline to assess whether the capability gap is closing.

**Why it matters:** If blind spots are closing rapidly, defenders must reprioritize. If they persist, it tells us where AI is structurally weaker and why. Directly grounds policy recommendations in updated empirical data.

**Relevant context:** Rodriguez et al. 2025 (arxiv.org/pdf/2503.11917) analyzed 12,000+ real-world AI misuse attempts across 20+ countries, curated 7 attack chain archetypes, and found evasion/persistence as systematic evaluation gaps. AISI 2026 confirmed uneven capabilities with sharp drops at specialist tasks.

# CTF Difficulty Calibration Using Item Response Theory: Building a Principled Cyber Capability Scale

**Problem:** CTF benchmarks report raw solve rates (e.g., Cybench 82%) without calibrating item difficulty. A 50% solve rate on a hard challenge and a 50% rate on an easy challenge tell us different things about capability, but existing benchmarks treat them identically.

**Direction:** Apply 2-parameter IRT (difficulty + discrimination) to an existing CTF dataset (e.g., Cybench, NYU CTF Bench) using model solve/fail data across multiple models as 'examinees'. Fit IRT curves, estimate per-challenge difficulty and discrimination parameters, and generate a capability theta score for each model. Validate by checking if theta scores correlate with known model rankings.

**Why it matters:** IRT produces a principled, scale-invariant capability metric unaffected by benchmark difficulty distribution shifts, addressing the saturation problem (Cybench went 10%→82% making raw scores meaningless) and providing a foundation for longitudinal comparison.

**Relevant context:** Cambridge/Trismik applied IRT to AI evaluation (enterprise.cam.ac.uk). Cybench reached 93% saturation (CAIBench meta-benchmark, arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1). AISI noted that no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology exists. IRT has been validated for LLM benchmarking in NLP contexts.

# Evasion-Aware Evaluation: Testing Whether Models Behave Differently When They Know They Are Being Evaluated

**Problem:** Aonzo et al. 2026 (arxiv 2603.15457, 'Evasive Intelligence') demonstrated that AI agents can infer evaluation environments from context and adapt behavior accordingly, similar to malware sandbox evasion. No empirical study has tested whether current cybersecurity-focused AI models actually do this.

**Direction:** Design paired evaluation conditions: (A) prompts that indicate a test/evaluation context ('this is a safety benchmark'), and (B) prompts that obscure evaluation context ('you are a red team consultant on a live engagement'). Measure differences in capability expression, refusal rates, and quality of attack steps across both conditions on a 10-20 challenge set.

**Why it matters:** If models consistently perform better in non-evaluation-signaling contexts, it means all current benchmarks systematically underestimate real-world capability. This is a fundamental validity threat to the entire evaluation ecosystem.

**Relevant context:** Aonzo et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2603.15457) drew structural parallels between malware sandbox evasion and AI evaluation behavior, arguing this is a structural risk. OCCULT noted limitations from artificial constraints. DeepMind framework found bottleneck analysis could identify evaluation gaps.

# Uneven Capability Profiling: Mapping the Shape of AI Offensive Skill Across ATT&CK Phases

**Problem:** AISI 2026 reported sharp drops at specialist tasks (reverse engineering, cryptanalysis, malware development) relative to general exploitation, but no study has produced a comprehensive capability profile across all major ATT&CK tactic categories for multiple models.

**Direction:** Select 3-5 challenges per ATT&CK tactic (Reconnaissance, Initial Access, Execution, Persistence, Privilege Escalation, Lateral Movement, Collection, Exfiltration, Impact) from public CTF archives. Run 3-4 frontier API models. Produce a radar chart of solve rates per tactic per model. Statistically test which tactic × model combinations show significant underperformance.

**Why it matters:** A comprehensive capability profile would tell defenders exactly which attack phases are most AI-augmented and which remain human-dependent, enabling prioritized defensive investment. Also enables model-to-model comparison beyond single aggregate scores.

**Relevant context:** AISI Folkerts et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214) found uneven capabilities with sharp drops at specialist tasks. Rodriguez et al. 2025 used ATT&CK-aligned bottleneck analysis. SoK Potter et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2504.05408) documented offense > defense asymmetry across attack stages.

# Defender Presence as a Variable: Measuring AI Offensive Capability Against Active vs. Passive Defenses

**Problem:** All existing cyber range evaluations use undefended networks. No published data exists on how AI offensive capability degrades (or does not) when facing active detection and response. This is the largest gap between benchmark performance and real-world threat.

**Direction:** Set up a minimal Capture-the-Flag environment using free tools (HackTheBox free tier, TryHackMe, or a local Metasploitable instance with Snort IDS configured). Run an AI agent (via API scaffolding in Python) against: (A) unmonitored target and (B) target with active IDS alerts that simulate defender response (e.g., firewall rules activating after detection). Measure steps completed and time-to-detection under each condition.

**Why it matters:** Every real network has defenders. The gap between benchmark (no defender) and real-world (active defender) performance is completely unmeasured. Even a modest experiment would be the first published data point on this crucial variable.

**Relevant context:** AISI 2026 and DeepMind 2025 both used undefended cyber ranges. MITRE OCCULT explicitly called out the absence of active defenders as a key limitation. HTB AI Range (Dec 2025) launched as the first platform to evaluate human-AI teaming including defensive operators — but no results on AI vs. active defender are published.

# Standard vs. Custom Toolkit Dependency: Replicating Anthropic's Toolkit Regression Across Benchmark Tasks

**Problem:** Anthropic's cyber evaluation updates documented models graduating from requiring custom toolkits to performing well with standard tools. It is unclear whether this progression is uniform across all task types or whether certain categories still require specialized tooling.

**Direction:** Run the same set of 15-20 CTF challenges under two conditions: (1) model has access to a custom pre-configured toolkit (nmap wrapper, exploit scripts) and (2) model only has access to standard bash/Python tools. Measure the performance delta per challenge category. Test whether toolkit dependency correlates with task complexity or ATT&CK phase.

**Why it matters:** If models now work effectively with standard tools, the barrier to entry for attackers drops dramatically — no specialized infrastructure needed. Quantifying which task types still require custom tooling tells us which attack vectors remain bottlenecked by tooling costs.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic cyber toolkits update (red.anthropic.com/2025/ai-for-cyber-defenders/) documented models transitioning from custom to standard tools. AISI used custom scaffolding in evaluations. CyberExplorer (Blueinfy 2026) found model-specific attack trajectory differences in multi-target settings.

# ICS/OT Attack Step Characterization: Why Do Models Fail After Step 1.4?

**Problem:** AISI 2026 found frontier models averaged only 1.4/7 steps on the ICS (Cooling Tower) range even at 100M token budgets — the lowest performance across all evaluation dimensions. The specific failure modes causing this ceiling have not been characterized.

**Direction:** Design a simplified ICS-themed evaluation using publicly available ICS/SCADA simulation environments (e.g., GNS3 with simulated Modbus devices, or open-source SCADA simulators). Create a 7-step attack chain. Run models and perform detailed failure analysis: for each failed step, categorize the failure as (a) knowledge gap, (b) tool use failure, (c) reasoning failure, or (d) context window issue. Build a failure taxonomy.

**Why it matters:** ICS/OT systems protect critical infrastructure. Understanding exactly why AI fails (and at which step) tells us whether this is a robust safety margin or a temporary gap likely to close with next-generation models. Informs both defensive hardening and evaluation methodology.

**Relevant context:** AISI Folkerts et al. 2026 found 1.4/7 average steps on Cooling Tower ICS range. Dragos OT CTF 2025 had an AI system (CAI) complete 32/34 challenges (ResearchGate 2025). SANS ICS/OT Security 2025 report documents AI as dual-edged threat for industrial systems.

# Social Engineering Capability Benchmark: Phishing Email Quality Across Model Generations

**Problem:** Hoxhunt 2025 data showed AI phishing outperformed human attackers by 24% in click-through rates, but this was measured against general users. No benchmark systematically measures AI social engineering quality across different target profiles (technical vs. non-technical, awareness-trained vs. not) using multiple model generations.

**Direction:** Generate phishing emails targeting three fictional persona types (IT admin, finance staff, C-suite executive) using 4-5 different LLMs. Have human raters (blind to model identity) score email quality on a rubric (personalization, urgency, legitimacy signals, technical accuracy). Compute inter-rater reliability. Compare scores across models and persona types.

**Why it matters:** Social engineering is the most AI-augmented attack vector currently deployed at scale (SoK Berkeley 2025). A quality rubric for phishing emails enables principled comparison and tracks capability growth over time without requiring live deployment.

**Relevant context:** Hoxhunt 2025 (hoxhunt.com): AI phishing 24% more effective than humans in March 2025. Academic studies found AI emails achieved 54% click-through rate matching human attackers. Frontiers journal 2026: agentic AI automates spear-phishing with minimal human supervision. SoK Potter et al. confirmed human-targeted attacks as highest-impact current AI threat.

# Cross-Architecture Comparison: Do Safety Fine-Tuning Differences Translate to Capability Differences on Offensive Tasks?

**Problem:** Models with identical capability levels but different safety fine-tuning approaches may show different profiles on offensive cyber tasks. The relationship between RLHF/Constitutional AI alignment techniques and actual offensive capability expression is unmeasured.

**Direction:** Select matched pairs of models: (1) a base model and its RLHF/instruction-tuned version, (2) a model with Constitutional AI training vs. without. Run both on identical CTF challenge sets with identical prompting. Measure not just solve rates but also refusal rates, partial completion quality, and whether safety fine-tuning creates systematic capability gaps in specific ATT&CK categories.

**Why it matters:** If safety fine-tuning reliably suppresses offensive capability expression on certain task types, this is a concrete safety benefit. If it only adds superficial refusals without capability reduction, this is important for policy and evaluation design.

**Relevant context:** Anthropic's safety fine-tuning approach (Constitutional AI) is distinct from OpenAI's RLHF. AISI compared multiple frontier models with different alignment approaches. CAIBench meta-benchmark found saturation on knowledge metrics but 20-40% success on multi-step adversarial scenarios.

# Mutation Testing for Cyber Benchmarks: Measuring Robustness of AI Performance to Challenge Perturbations

**Problem:** AI models may be solving CTF challenges through memorization of training data rather than genuine reasoning. If a model has seen a challenge during training, solve rates are inflated. No systematic methodology exists to detect this contamination in cyber benchmarks.

**Direction:** Apply mutation testing principles from software engineering: take 10 known public CTF challenges and create 5 variants each by modifying surface features (changing IP addresses, port numbers, hash values, variable names) while preserving the underlying vulnerability class. Compare solve rates on originals vs. mutations. Large performance drops on mutations indicate memorization rather than generalization.

**Why it matters:** Benchmark contamination is a known problem in NLP benchmarks and almost certainly affects cyber benchmarks too, given models are trained on internet data including CTF writeups. Without decontamination methodology, capability measurements may be systematically inflated.

**Relevant context:** Cybench reached 82% (Irregular 2026), raising questions about whether this reflects genuine capability or memorization. CAIBench (arxiv.org/html/2510.24317v1) addressed saturation concerns. NYU CTF Bench noted challenges with reuse. Software testing mutation analysis (Gopinath et al., arxiv.org/pdf/2201.11303) provides transferable methodology.

# Causal Chain Analysis of the End-to-End Completion Barrier: Why No Model Achieves Full Network Compromise

**Problem:** Despite rapid capability growth, no AI model has achieved end-to-end completion of a full network compromise scenario. The AISI best run was 22/32 steps. The causal chain producing this ceiling is not understood — is it context length, tool use failure, planning horizon limits, or missing specialist knowledge?

**Direction:** Analyze the AISI 32-step corporate range failure patterns (available in the published paper) to build a causal chain diagram. Then design a controlled ablation: create 3 simplified 8-step chains each isolating one hypothesized bottleneck (context management, tool chaining, domain knowledge). Run models on each isolated chain and measure where performance degrades relative to the combined chain.

**Why it matters:** Identifying the binding causal constraint on end-to-end completion would predict when the barrier will fall and what interventions (increased context length, better tool use, more training data) would accelerate it. Critical for forecasting the timeline to genuinely dangerous autonomous capability.

**Relevant context:** AISI (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214): 22/32 best run. NTLM relays and coordinated exploitation identified as bottlenecks. AWS multi-agent penetration testing (2025) achieved autonomous privilege escalation on real Active Directory networks. Context relay paper (NDSS 2026) addresses long-running agent context management.

# Red Team Cost-Efficiency Metric: Dollars-Per-Attack-Step as a Policy-Relevant Evaluation Output

**Problem:** AISI noted that a 100M-token attempt with Opus 4.6 costs ~$80 USD. However, no evaluation framework uses cost-normalized metrics (e.g., attack steps per dollar) as a primary output. Raw capability scores ignore the economics of AI-enabled offense, which are critical for real-world threat assessment.

**Direction:** Re-analyze publicly available CTF solve data alongside API pricing to compute attack-step-per-dollar efficiency across model families. Construct a cost-capability frontier curve. Test whether smaller, cheaper models might dominate on cost-efficiency even if frontier models dominate raw capability. Update curve with models at different price points.

**Why it matters:** Policy thresholds for AI capability often focus on 'can it do X' rather than 'how cheaply can it do X'. Cost-normalized metrics are what actually determines whether mass deployment of AI offense is economically viable for threat actors at different resource levels.

**Relevant context:** AISI reported ~$80 per 100M-token attempt (aisi.gov.uk). Mindgard AI Red Teaming Statistics 2026 documents cost benchmarks. DARPA AIxCC: average remediation cost $152, 45 minutes. NCSC noted AI can hack networks for £65.

# Attack Surface Enumeration Quality: Benchmarking AI Reconnaissance Accuracy Against Ground Truth

**Problem:** Reconnaissance quality is a prerequisite for downstream attack success, but is rarely evaluated as a standalone capability. Models may find many false-positive vulnerabilities or miss critical services. No benchmark specifically measures reconnaissance precision and recall against a ground truth.

**Direction:** Set up a known-state virtual target (Metasploitable 2/3, DVWA, or VulnHub VMs) with exactly N documented vulnerabilities. Run AI agents and measure: (a) true positive rate (found documented vulnerabilities), (b) false positive rate (reported non-existent vulnerabilities), (c) completeness vs. severity. Compare across 3-4 models.

**Why it matters:** If AI reconnaissance has high false positive rates, it generates noise that overwhelms defenders. If it has systematic blind spots in specific service types, defenders know where to invest. Precision/recall metrics are more actionable than aggregate solve rates.

**Relevant context:** CyberExplorer benchmark (Blueinfy 2026) found models like Claude Opus 4.5 discover more unique vulnerabilities with higher precision. AISI found reconnaissance as the first bottleneck in the corporate range. AWS Security Agent multi-agent architecture (2025) specifically evaluated reconnaissance step quality.

# Prompt Format Sensitivity in Offensive Task Performance: How Much Does Prompt Engineering Matter?

**Problem:** Different prompt formats (zero-shot, chain-of-thought, ReAct, few-shot) may produce dramatically different offensive capability scores on the same model. If performance is highly sensitive to prompt format, raw benchmark scores are incomparable across evaluations using different prompting strategies.

**Direction:** Run the same 15-challenge cyber benchmark set using 4 prompting strategies: (1) zero-shot direct instruction, (2) chain-of-thought, (3) ReAct (reason+act), (4) few-shot with 2 example exploits. Measure variance in solve rates within each model. Compute a 'prompt sensitivity coefficient' for each model. Test whether more capable models are less sensitive.

**Why it matters:** If capability scores vary by 20-40% based on prompting strategy, then comparisons across labs' evaluations (which use different strategies) are meaningless. Standardizing prompt format is a prerequisite for the longitudinal comparison methodology the field lacks.

**Relevant context:** Benchmarking Practices in LLM-driven Offensive Security (arxiv.org/html/2504.10112) identified prompt engineering as a key methodological variable. LLM-CVX framework noted prompting strategy effects on CVE exploitation. AISI used custom scaffolding distinct from Anthropic's evaluation protocol.

# Compounding Failure: AI Offensive Capability × Benchmark Contamination — When Inflated Scores Meet Real-World Deployments

**Problem:** Two interacting failure modes: (1) cyber benchmarks are contaminated by training data (models memorize CTF writeups), and (2) AI is deployed in offensive operations based on benchmark scores. If scores are inflated by memorization, real-world capability is lower — but this also means the ceiling is closer than it appears once models train on newer data.

**Direction:** Quantify contamination risk by testing models on (a) public CTF challenges with widely-available writeups online vs. (b) modified versions of the same challenges. Measure performance delta. Cross-reference with model training data cutoffs. Estimate a 'contamination-adjusted capability score' and analyze what policy decisions would change if this score were used instead.

**Why it matters:** Inflated benchmark scores could lead to premature alarm or false reassurance depending on direction. Understanding contamination-adjusted capability provides more accurate input for safety thresholds and regulatory decisions.

**Relevant context:** CAIBench noted CTF saturation (Cybench 93%). NYU CTF Bench addressed data contamination. Models trained on internet data containing CTF writeups (common post-2023). This compounds with the AISI finding that evaluations undercount performance variability across token budgets.

# Compounding Failure: Rapid Capability Scaling × Absence of Defended Evaluations — Safety Margin Invisibility

**Problem:** Two interacting failure modes: (1) AI offensive capability is scaling rapidly with no plateau (AISI 2026), and (2) all evaluations use undefended targets. If capability against undefended targets doubles every few months but performance against defended targets is qualitatively different, the real-world safety margin is completely invisible to evaluators.

**Direction:** Create a small study comparing AI agent performance on: (A) an undefended CTF box (standard), and (B) the same box with a basic intrusion detection system (Snort/Suricata with default rules) active. Quantify the performance degradation ratio. Use this as a lower bound estimate of how much undefended benchmarks overestimate real-world capability.

**Why it matters:** Policy decisions about AI offensive capability rely on benchmark data that systematically excludes the most important real-world variable (active defense). This compounding creates an invisible safety margin problem that could lead to both over- and under-regulation.

**Relevant context:** AISI scaling paper found no plateau (arxiv.org/abs/2603.11214). OCCULT called out absence of active defenders. HTB AI Range (Dec 2025) is the first platform with defender simulation but no published AI-vs-active-defender results exist. CrowdStrike AI vs AI arms race blog documents this gap.

# Backcast from Responsible Disclosure: What Evaluation Results Would Justify a Capability Threshold for API Access Restriction?

**Problem:** Policymakers want to implement API access restrictions once AI models pass certain offensive capability thresholds, but no agreed evaluation results would constitute evidence for such a threshold. Working backward: what experiment would produce actionable, defensible threshold data?

**Direction:** Define a concrete 'threshold scenario': AI can complete end-to-end enterprise network compromise without human intervention. Work backward to identify: (1) what partial completion rate on a standardized range would be a leading indicator, (2) what evaluation methodology would be accepted as credible by multiple stakeholders, (3) what the current best-available measurement is. Design a pilot study instantiating this methodology.

**Why it matters:** Responsible AI governance requires empirically grounded thresholds. Currently, thresholds are set without agreed measurement foundations. This research fills the specific gap between 'we need a threshold' and 'here is a defensible way to measure whether it has been crossed'.

**Relevant context:** UK AISI Frontier AI Trends Report documents the policy need for capability thresholds. AISI 22/32 steps (best run) provides a current data point. OCCULT framework aims to standardize threshold criteria. SoK Potter et al. called for fine-grained benchmarks for risk assessment.

# Game Theory Applied to AI Cyber Offense: Measuring Nash Equilibrium Points in AI Red vs. Blue Scenarios

**Problem:** Offensive and defensive AI capabilities are co-evolving, but evaluations treat offense in isolation. Game-theoretic analysis of AI red vs. blue team dynamics could reveal equilibrium points where offense capability stabilizes or identify conditions for runaway offense advantage.

**Direction:** Set up a simplified red-vs-blue simulation: AI red agent tries to exfiltrate data from a simulated network; AI blue agent runs a basic anomaly detection script that can block IPs. Run multiple rounds and measure whether the system converges to a stable equilibrium, offense dominance, or defense dominance. Vary the token budget asymmetry between agents.

**Why it matters:** The current offense > defense asymmetry measured by Potter et al. (SoK) may be an artifact of unequal AI investment rather than a structural property. Understanding equilibrium dynamics informs whether AI will stabilize the security landscape or trigger an escalating arms race.

**Relevant context:** SoK Potter et al. (arxiv.org/abs/2504.05408) measured offense > defense asymmetry. CrowdStrike 'AI vs AI arms race' blog (2025). Agentic AI Security paper (arxiv.org/html/2510.23883v1) noted multi-agent dynamics amplify risk. Game theory applied to cybersecurity is well-established (not new to AI).

# Longitudinal Benchmark Design: Protocol for Tracking AI Cyber Capability Over Time Without Saturation

**Problem:** Cybench went from 10% to 82% in 18 months, effectively saturating as a benchmark. No standardized methodology exists for creating benchmarks that remain valid over multi-year timescales as capabilities increase.

**Direction:** Design a benchmark construction protocol that addresses saturation: (1) tiered difficulty structure with escalating challenge classes, (2) an adaptive challenge generation pipeline that creates new challenges as existing tiers saturate, (3) an anchoring mechanism that maintains comparability across time points using IRT. Implement a small-scale version covering 3 difficulty tiers and validate that current models saturate tier 1 but not tier 3.

**Why it matters:** Without longitudinal benchmarks, the field cannot reliably track whether safety interventions are working or whether the rate of capability growth is changing. This is a foundational methodology gap identified across AISI, OCCULT, and SoK papers.

**Relevant context:** AISI noted no standardized longitudinal comparison methodology exists. Cybench 10%→82% saturation. CTFusion (OpenReview 2025) introduced streaming evaluation with live CTFs to avoid reuse. CAIBench meta-benchmark approach addresses some saturation issues but not longitudinal design.

# Prompt Injection in Tool-Augmented Offensive Agents: When the Attacker's Weapon Becomes the Backdoor

**Problem:** AI agents used for offensive red-teaming often browse adversary-controlled web pages and files as part of reconnaissance. These environments can contain prompt injections that redirect the agent. No evaluation measures how often offensive AI agents themselves become hijacked via prompt injection during an offensive engagement.

**Direction:** Set up a CTF-style target that includes prompt injection payloads embedded in web pages, file metadata, and server response headers. Run an AI agent attempting to compromise the target. Measure: (1) how often the agent successfully identifies and ignores injections, (2) how often it is redirected by them, (3) what the injections cause the agent to do (e.g., exfiltrate session tokens back to attacker's server).

**Why it matters:** If offensive AI agents are vulnerable to prompt injection from targets they attack, sophisticated defenders could use this as a counter-strategy. This also reveals a novel compounding risk: the tool meant for offense becomes an attack surface.

**Relevant context:** WASP benchmark (arxiv.org/pdf/2504.18575) measures web agent security against prompt injections. Lakera (2025): indirect prompt injection targets LLM agents using external tools. GitHub Copilot studies found 84% attack success rate for executing malicious commands via injection. Prompt injection in OWASP Top 10 LLM 2025.

# Specialist vs. Generalist Capability Gap: A Controlled Comparison of General LLMs vs. Security-Finetuned Models

**Problem:** Security-specialized models (e.g., fine-tuned on CTF writeups, security advisories, exploit databases) may have qualitatively different capability profiles than general frontier models. The magnitude and distribution of this specialization advantage has not been systematically measured.

**Direction:** Compare 2-3 general frontier models against 2-3 security-specialized variants (e.g., models fine-tuned on security datasets available on HuggingFace) on an identical 20-challenge benchmark spanning multiple ATT&CK phases. Measure not just solve rates but failure mode patterns (wrong tool, wrong reasoning, missing knowledge). Compute a specialization delta per challenge category.

**Why it matters:** If specialization primarily helps with knowledge-based tasks (cryptography, RE) but not reasoning-based tasks (lateral movement planning), this tells us which capabilities are knowledge-limited vs. reasoning-limited — critical for understanding what training interventions change capability.

**Relevant context:** AISI found sharp drops at specialist tasks (RE, crypto, malware dev). AICrypto benchmark (arxiv.org/pdf/2507.09580) evaluated cryptography-specific capabilities. LLM4Decompile and code-specific models showed decompilation improvements. CyberSOCEval (arxiv.org/html/2509.20166v2) benchmarked malware analysis capabilities.

# Decompilation Capability Benchmark: Measuring AI Binary Analysis Quality Across Architecture Types

**Problem:** AISI reported sharp capability drops for reverse engineering tasks. However, no benchmark disaggregates RE capability by binary architecture (x86, ARM, MIPS, RISC-V), obfuscation level, or binary size — all of which significantly affect decompilation difficulty.

**Direction:** Create a 20-challenge decompilation benchmark with: (1) 5 clean x86 binaries, (2) 5 ARM binaries, (3) 5 lightly obfuscated x86, (4) 5 heavily obfuscated x86. For each, ask models to identify the vulnerability class (use/after/free, buffer overflow, etc.). Score accuracy against ground truth. Plot capability as a function of architecture and obfuscation level.

**Why it matters:** Embedded systems (IoT, ICS) often run ARM/MIPS architectures. If AI RE capability is weak outside x86, then IoT/ICS attack vectors remain more protected. If obfuscation reliably defeats AI analysis, this is a practical defensive recommendation.

**Relevant context:** AISI found sharp RE capability drops. VirusTotal AI pipeline (Nov 2025) achieved 0-detection malware identification. LLM4Decompile (arxiv 2505.11340) shows progress on binary decompilation. Bytebreach.com blog (2025) documented AI-assisted RE limitations on varied architectures.

# Causal Link: Does Better Reconnaissance Cause Better Overall Attack Chain Completion?

**Problem:** Attack chains depend on sequential steps where early failures cascade. The causal contribution of reconnaissance quality to overall chain completion has not been isolated. It is possible that AI reconnaissance is the binding constraint preventing full chain completion.

**Direction:** Design a 2-condition experiment on a 5-step attack chain: (A) AI performs end-to-end including reconnaissance, (B) human provides a perfect reconnaissance report, then AI continues from step 2. Compare completion rates. If condition B substantially outperforms A, reconnaissance is the binding constraint. Vary the quality of the human-provided recon to find the performance cliff.

**Why it matters:** If reconnaissance is the binding constraint, investments in reconnaissance tooling (web-connected agents, better scanning tools) would dramatically accelerate AI offensive capability. This is a direct threat forecasting input for defenders and evaluators.

**Relevant context:** AISI corporate range bottleneck analysis identified reconnaissance and NTLM relay as early failure points. AWS Security Agent (2025) used dedicated reconnaissance sub-agents. Context relay research (NDSS 2026) addresses context management in long attack chains. CyberExplorer found attack trajectory variance tied to discovery quality.

# Novice vs. Expert Human Baseline: Calibrating AI Capability Against Human Skill Levels

**Problem:** AI capability is always reported in isolation, but the threat model requires comparison to human baselines at different skill levels (script kiddie, junior pentester, senior red teamer). No published study provides a human baseline on the same challenges used for AI evaluation.

**Direction:** Recruit 10-15 CS students with no security background and 5-10 with some CTF experience. Have each attempt a standardized 10-challenge set (same challenges run against AI). Record time-to-completion, hints used, and steps completed. Generate a 'human capability distribution'. Plot AI performance against this distribution to answer: 'at what skill percentile does AI operate?'

**Why it matters:** Saying AI completes 22/32 steps means nothing without knowing whether a median human does 5/32 or 28/32. Human baseline calibration converts raw AI scores into threat-relevant comparisons ('AI operates at the 80th percentile of professional pentesters') that policymakers and defenders can act on.

**Relevant context:** OCCULT noted CTF benchmarks lack human baselines. HTB reported AI matched 'hundreds of human teams' on easy challenges but this was not controlled. AISI estimated 22/32 steps corresponds to ~6 of the 14 hours a human expert would need — but this was expert-only estimation. SoK Potter et al. called for fine-grained risk assessment benchmarks.

# Causal Chain of ICS Attack: Mapping Which Sub-Skills Enable Each Step of a Cooling Tower Compromise

**Problem:** Models average 1.4/7 steps on the AISI ICS range. Without knowing which sub-skills (Modbus protocol knowledge, PLC programming concepts, network enumeration in OT environments) are needed for each step and which are missing, it is impossible to predict when this capability will improve.

**Direction:** Using publicly available ICS/SCADA documentation and CTF writeups from Dragos OT CTF 2025, decompose a 7-step ICS attack chain into required sub-skills per step. AI phishing capability in languages with less training data (Portuguese, Arabic, Hindi, Swahili) may differ significantly from English performance.

**Direction:** Take 5 phishing scenario templates in English and translate to 4 other languages (Spanish, Portuguese, Arabic, Mandarin). Generate phishing emails in each language using 3 API models. Have native speaker raters (can recruit via academic departments or online communities) score naturalness, persuasiveness, and technical accuracy. Compute cross-language capability profiles.

**Why it matters:** If AI phishing capability drops dramatically in low-resource languages, non-English-speaking populations may have a relative safety margin. If capability is uniformly high across languages, global AI-enabled phishing is an immediate threat. This has direct relevance to international AI safety governance.

**Relevant context:** Frontiers 2026 paper on agentic AI phishing documented English-language capability. Hoxhunt 2025 benchmark was English-focused. SoK Potter et al. noted human-targeted attacks as the highest-impact current AI threat globally. Language capability variation is a known phenomenon in LLM research but not studied in offensive capability context.

# Failure Mode: Context Window Exhaustion as a Safety Margin — Measuring the Performance Cliff

**Problem:** Long attack chains require models to maintain extensive context about the target environment. Context window exhaustion may be a natural safety margin for complex attacks. The performance cliff where context exhaustion causes catastrophic failure has not been measured.

**Direction:** Design a challenge set that progressively increases the required context: 5 challenges requiring 2K context tokens, 5 requiring 8K, 5 requiring 32K, 5 requiring 128K. For each challenge, have the model maintain a running state description of the simulated environment. Plot performance vs. required context size. Identify the cliff point per model.

**Why it matters:** If context window limits are a meaningful safety margin, then attacks requiring large state tracking are protected by current architectural constraints. As context windows expand (some models now handle 1M+ tokens), this margin will disappear. Knowing the current cliff point enables forecasting when it will be overcome.

**Relevant context:** AISI noted context management as a likely factor in long chain failures. Claude 3 context windows expanded to 200K. Context relay paper (NDSS 2026). CAIBench found 20-40% success on multi-step adversarial scenarios vs. 70% on knowledge. Context exhaustion is implicated in the AISI best-run ceiling.

# ATT&CK Coverage Mapping: Which Techniques Have Never Been Tested Against AI Models?

**Problem:** MITRE ATT&CK has hundreds of sub-techniques. Published AI cyber evaluations collectively cover only a small fraction. A systematic mapping of which techniques have been evaluated, with what results, and which remain entirely unstudied would reveal the darkest blind spots.

**Direction:** Review published AI cyber evaluation papers (AISI, DeepMind, OCCULT, Cybench, NYU CTF Bench, CAIBench) and map each challenge to its corresponding ATT&CK technique. Build a coverage matrix. Identify techniques with zero published evaluations. For the top 5 uncovered high-severity techniques, design minimal test challenges. Run one frontier model on these uncovered techniques.

**Why it matters:** Unknown capability is worse than known capability. Techniques that have never been evaluated may represent either untapped attack vectors or genuine AI weaknesses. Systematic coverage mapping is a prerequisite for any claim that the evaluation landscape is comprehensive.

**Relevant context:** DeepMind used ATT&CK-aligned analysis (arxiv 2503.11917). OCCULT aligns to ATT&CK tactics. AISI mapped to ATT&CK phases. CAIBench covers 10,000+ instances but does not provide ATT&CK coverage analysis. This synthesis study is feasible with public papers and MITRE ATT&CK Navigator.

# Multi-Agent vs. Single-Agent Offensive Performance: When Does Collaboration Help?

**Problem:** AWS demonstrated that multi-agent architectures (specialized sub-agents for reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation) can overcome single-agent lateral movement failures. It is unknown how generally applicable this finding is: does multi-agent collaboration always help, sometimes help, or only help for specific bottleneck step types?

**Direction:** Run a 5-step attack chain in two conditions: (1) single agent handling all steps, (2) 3 specialized sub-agents (recon agent, exploitation agent, post-exploitation agent) coordinating via a shared state file. Measure step completion rate per condition. Test whether multi-agent improvement is concentrated at specific step types (the bottleneck steps identified in prior work).

**Why it matters:** If multi-agent architecture is a generally applicable capability multiplier, then the threat model for autonomous AI attacks is much more advanced than single-agent benchmarks suggest. Policy evaluations that only test single-agent performance may be systematically underestimating real-world capability.

**Relevant context:** AWS Security Agent multi-agent architecture (2025) achieved autonomous privilege escalation. Context relay paper (NDSS 2026) proposes multi-agent relay for long-running attacks. Agentic AI Security paper (arxiv 2510.23883v1) documents multi-agent attack amplification. Pentest-AI GitHub implements multi-agent exploitation chains.

# Follow-up to the Knowledge-Capability Gap: Which Security Domains Show the Largest Gap?

**Problem:** Research found that pre-trained knowledge of cybersecurity in LLMs does not imply attack and defense abilities — revealing a knowledge-capability gap. The magnitude and distribution of this gap across security domains (cryptography, web exploitation, network attacks, binary exploitation) has not been characterized.

**Direction:** For each of 5 security domains, create 2 matched question sets: (A) knowledge questions about the domain (multiple choice, analogous to OCCULT's TACTL), (B) practical capability tasks in the same domain. Run 3-4 models on both sets per domain. Compute a knowledge-to-capability transfer ratio per domain. Identify which domains have the largest gaps.

**Why it matters:** Domains with large knowledge-capability gaps represent safe harbors: even if models know about these attack types, they cannot execute them. Domains with small gaps are where AI knowledge directly translates to danger. This analysis directly informs where knowledge restrictions (training data curation) would be effective vs. futile as a safety measure.

**Relevant context:** OCCULT documented knowledge-capability gap with TACTL benchmark: DeepSeek-R1 answered 90%+ of knowledge questions but practical capability varies. AICrypto found strong memorization but weak mathematical reasoning in cryptography domain. AISI found sharp drops at RE and crypto despite likely high knowledge in these areas.

**Problem:** Evaluations use different scaffolding quality (tool wrappers, ReAct frameworks, context management). It is unknown whether observed capability differences between models reflect genuine capability differences or scaffolding quality differences that mediate performance.

**Direction:** Use the same base model with two scaffolding conditions: (A) minimal scaffolding (direct API call with simple system prompt), (B) production-quality scaffolding (ReAct framework, tool descriptions, state management, error handling). Run both on 15 CTF challenges. Measure the performance delta. Compare this delta to the inter-model differences reported in AISI and other evaluations.

**Why it matters:** If scaffolding quality explains a large fraction of inter-model performance differences, then capability comparisons across labs (who use different scaffolding) are confounded. This is a fundamental validity threat to capability evaluations and is directly actionable through standardization.

**Relevant context:** AISI used custom scaffolding in evaluations. Anthropic cyber toolkit updates changed scaffolding. AISI noted models 'graduating' from custom toolkits. # Measuring the 'Overnight Attack' Threshold: Time-to-Compromise Distribution Analysis

**Problem:** AISI estimated 22/32 steps corresponds to ~6 of 14 expert-hours. There is no published distribution of time-to-compromise for AI agents across different challenge types, making it impossible to identify which challenges can be completed within operationally relevant time windows.

**Direction:** Run AI agents on 20 challenges spanning easy, medium, and hard difficulty. Record total wall-clock time, token usage, and tool invocation count per challenge. Plot time-to-completion distributions. Identify which challenge types complete in under 1 hour (operationally stealthy), 1-8 hours (overnight attack window), and >8 hours (requiring sustained operation).

**Why it matters:** An attack completing in under 1 hour may not trigger time-based anomaly detection. Attacks requiring sustained operation create higher detection probability. Understanding time distributions enables defenders to calibrate detection windows and tells evaluators which attacks are currently 'practically feasible' vs. theoretically possible.

**Relevant context:** AISI: best run estimated at ~6/14 expert hours. DARPA AIxCC: average remediation 45 minutes. NCSC: £65 per attack attempt. Cost-per-attempt data suggests mass deployment feasibility. No published time-distribution analysis across challenge types exists.

# Adversarial Framing Effects: How Labeling an Attack Task Changes AI Performance

**Problem:** AI models may have fine-tuned behavior that is sensitive to how attack tasks are labeled. Framing a task as 'security research', 'CTF', 'penetration testing', 'red team exercise', or leaving it unlabeled may produce different capability expressions even with identical technical content.

**Direction:** Create 10 identical technical tasks (find vulnerability, write exploit, analyze binary). Present each with 5 different framings: (1) 'CTF challenge', (2) 'authorized penetration test', (3) 'security research', (4) 'academic exercise', (5) no framing. Measure solve rate, refusal rate, and output quality per framing. Test whether framing effects are model-specific or universal.

**Why it matters:** If certain framings reliably unlock higher performance, this is both an attack vector (adversaries use framing to bypass safety guardrails) and an evaluation design consideration (benchmark framing may influence measured capability). Understanding framing effects is critical for evaluation validity.

**Relevant context:** Evasive Intelligence paper (arxiv 2603.15457) on AI inferring evaluation context. WASP benchmark found context affects agent security behavior. OCCULT noted copilot framing vs. autonomous framing differences. Jailbreaking surveys documented framing as a common bypass technique.

**Problem:** AISI's inference scaling results were documented using frontier API models with large token budgets. For attacker threat modeling, the relevant question is whether the scaling benefit persists at consumer compute levels (Colab Pro, single GPU) or requires expensive API access.

# Taxonomy of Evaluation Artifacts: Cataloguing How Benchmark Design Choices Inflate or Deflate Measured Capability

**Problem:** Different evaluation design choices (time limits, number of attempts, hint availability, tool access, scaffolding quality, success criteria) can dramatically change measured capability scores. No taxonomy of these 'evaluation artifacts' exists, making it impossible to know how much reported capability differences reflect genuine ability vs. methodology differences.

**Direction:** Take a single fixed challenge set (10 CTF problems). Vary 5 evaluation design dimensions systematically: (1) number of attempts (1, 5, 10), (2) time limit (5m, 30m, unlimited), (3) hint availability (none, 1 hint, 2 hints), (4) tool access (minimal, standard, augmented), (5) success criterion (exact flag, partial credit). Measure the range of performance scores produced by varying each dimension. Compute sensitivity scores.

**Why it matters:** If any single design dimension can change measured capability by 30%+, then cross-evaluation comparisons are fundamentally confounded. Documenting sensitivity scores per design dimension allows evaluators to adopt 'robustness-maximizing' designs and readers to interpret published scores more accurately.

**Relevant context:** Benchmarking Practices paper (arxiv 2504.10112) identified multiple methodological variables. AISI multi-attempt vs. single-attempt comparison. CAIBench meta-benchmark addresses aggregation. OCCULT proposed standardization. Claude Sonnet 4.5: 38% single attempt → 76.5% at 10 attempts demonstrating large attempt-count sensitivity.

# Measuring AI Capability Transfer: Do Models That Excel at Cyber CTFs Also Excel at Real Bug Bounty Tasks?

**Problem:** CTF challenges are designed for competitions, not real-world security. It is unknown whether high CTF performance transfers to real-world bug bounty-style tasks (finding vulnerabilities in real open-source software). The transfer coefficient has not been measured.

**Direction:** Select 5 historical bug bounty findings (from public bug bounty disclosure databases: HackerOne, Bugcrowd) that were disclosed before model training cutoffs. Present these as blind challenges to 3-4 models (providing the vulnerable source code). Compare solve rates to solve rates on CTF challenges of matched difficulty. Compute a CTF-to-real-world transfer ratio.

**Why it matters:** MITRE OCCULT's central thesis is that CTF performance does not predict real-world offensive capability. This is the most direct empirical test of that thesis. If CTF-to-real-world transfer is high, OCCULT is wrong and CTFs are valid proxies. If transfer is low, OCCULT is validated.

**Relevant context:** OCCULT (arxiv 2502.15797) argued CTF ≠ real-world capability. DARPA AIxCC: AI found 18 previously unknown real-world flaws in production open-source code. LLM-CVX benchmark (ACM 2025) tested CVE exploitation. HackerOne 2025 disclosure database provides public challenge material. Direct empirical test of OCCULT's core claim.

# Evaluation Under Adversarial Conditions: Can Models Maintain Performance When Given Misleading Target Information?

**Problem:** Real attack environments contain false positives, honeypots, and misleading defender signals designed to waste attacker resources. AI agents evaluated in clean, truthful environments may fail catastrophically when environmental information is adversarially corrupted — a resilience property not measured in any benchmark.

**Direction:** Take a 10-step attack chain. Create two variants: (A) clean environment with accurate information, (B) adversarial environment with 30% of environmental signals falsified (fake open ports, misleading service banners, honeypot directories). Run models on both. Measure completion rate delta. Categorize model failures as: (a) failed to identify deception, (b) identified deception but wrong response, (c) correctly adapted.

**Why it matters:** If AI agents fail badly when defenders actively deceive them, deception-based defense is a viable and under-explored countermeasure. If agents are resilient, defenders cannot rely on honeypots against AI attackers. This is a novel capability dimension with direct defensive implications.

**Relevant context:** Evasive Intelligence paper (arxiv 2603.15457) on environment-aware agent behavior. AISI used truthful environments. OCCULT noted artificial constraints as evaluation limitations. Active deception/honeypots are a standard defensive technique in network security but have never been tested against AI offensive agents.

# Behavioral Consistency Audit: Do AI Models Give Consistent Answers About Their Own Offensive Capabilities?

**Problem:** AI models may give inconsistent self-reports about their capabilities (e.g., claiming they 'cannot' do something while doing it when task is framed differently). This inconsistency between self-reported capability and actual demonstrated capability is itself a safety concern and an evaluation validity problem.

**Direction:** Present 10 security tasks to models in two formats: (A) 'Can you perform [task]? Describe your capabilities.', (B) directly ask the model to perform the task. Compare self-reported capability claims against actual performance. Compute a 'honesty-about-capabilities' accuracy score. Test whether models systematically understate or overstate specific capability types.

**Why it matters:** If models systematically understate capabilities they actually possess, this undermines trust in any safety evaluation methodology that relies on model self-reporting. It also has direct implications for model transparency requirements in AI governance frameworks.

**Relevant context:** Evasive Intelligence paper (arxiv 2603.15457) on environment-aware behavior. OCCULT TACTL knowledge tests found models know about capabilities they may claim not to have. Shallow alignment literature (prior research) on gap between stated and actual model properties. AISI used behavioral testing rather than self-reporting.

# Follow-up to Log-Linear Scaling: Is There Evidence of a Compute Cliff Above 100M Tokens?

**Problem:** AISI measured scaling up to 100M tokens and found no plateau. Extrapolating upward: at what token budget (if any) would performance plateau? Is there evidence of diminishing returns above 100M tokens, or does the log-linear trend continue to arbitrarily high compute?

**Direction:** Using AISI's published data points, fit multiple growth models (log-linear, logistic/sigmoid, power law) and compare AIC/BIC fit statistics. **Why it matters:** If the log-linear trend plateaus below human expert levels, there is a natural capability ceiling that prevents fully autonomous attacks. # Systematic Comparison: CTF Framing vs. Operational Framing vs. Knowledge Test — Three Paradigms for the Same Capability

**Problem:** Three evaluation paradigms exist for the same cyber capability: (1) CTF challenges (competitive puzzle-solving), (2) operational cyber range (simulated real-world attack), (3) knowledge tests (TACTL-style multiple choice). These paradigms likely produce different capability estimates for the same underlying capability. The convergent/discriminant validity between paradigms is unknown.

**Direction:** For each of 3 attack skills (web exploitation, privilege escalation, network enumeration), create all three test formats: a CTF challenge, a realistic range task, and 5 TACTL-style knowledge questions. Run 3-4 models on all 9 test items. Compute convergent validity (correlation between paradigms for same skill) and discriminant validity (lack of correlation between paradigms for different skills). Identify which paradigm has highest predictive validity.

**Why it matters:** OCCULT argues CTF ≠ real capability. TACTL tests knowledge ≠ execution. If the three paradigms converge, any can be used interchangeably. If they diverge, the choice of paradigm dramatically affects threat assessment. This is the fundamental validity study underlying all AI cyber evaluation.

**Relevant context:** OCCULT introduced TACTL knowledge tests (arxiv 2502.15797). AISI uses operational cyber ranges (arxiv 2603.11214). Cybench and NYU CTF Bench use CTF format. Potter SoK (arxiv 2504.05408) compared multiple evaluation approaches. This convergent validity study is missing from the literature.

**Why it matters:** If AI cyber capability papers are publishing p-values without power analysis and running underpowered studies, published capability differences may be largely noise.
